I've written notes on the verses I could support from pages I actually read. Coverage is uneven, so here are the gaps first:

- **Searches cut off early.** The search tool hit its usage limit after only a few searches and page reads.
- **Long pages were cut short.** Enduring Word's full Psalm 119 page stopped partway through v. 9, and the NET Bible page stopped before most of its notes.
- **vv. 17–29 are thin.** They rely mostly on short search-result excerpts, Chuck Smith's survey on StudyLight, and NET's translation.
- **Sites I never reached:** the Catholic and Orthodox sites (newadvent.org, catholic.com, oca.org), the Lutheran sites, bibleodyssey.org, gotquestions.org and the Pentecostal sites other than Enduring Word.
- **Popular modern teaching:** I found nothing on prosperity, word of faith or hyper-grace readings of these verses, so that part is left out.

---

## Introduction (whole psalm)

- **Form.** It is an acrostic: 22 eight-verse sections, one for each Hebrew letter, and every line in a section begins with that letter. The author isn't named. Older commentators mostly said David; some modern ones date it after the exile (Ezra or Nehemiah's time). Guzik says we can't be sure and don't need to know. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-119/
- **Eight words for God's word.** Law, word, judgments, testimonies, commandments, statutes, precepts, and a second word for "word." God's written word is mentioned in at least 171 of the 176 verses. Guzik quotes Kidner: every mention of Scripture is tied directly to its Author, and from v. 4 on the psalm is addressed to God as prayer. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-119/
- **Clarke (Methodist) on the old readings.** The Greek church fathers read the psalm as a summary of David's life. The Latin fathers found in it the whole moral teaching of the Gospel. Most careful interpreters date it to the Babylonian captivity, but Clarke leans toward David, or toward David's notes. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/119-1.html
- **A modern view on structure.** Coffman thinks the acrostic leads the writer to string together unrelated thoughts. He mentions Briggs's idea that the synonyms once meant different types of Hebrew law, and takes them all as referring to the Bible's teaching. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/119-1.html
- **Fleming (Bridgeway).** "Law" here means all of God's instruction, not just the legal code of Moses. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/119-1.html

## Aleph (vv. 1–8)

**v. 1**
- **Guzik:** Living undefiled is a blessing, not a bore. Walking in God's law is what being undefiled means, and some parts of a pure life can only be learned from Scripture. He quotes Spurgeon: blessedness needs steady forward movement, not just sitting still and staying clean. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-119/
- **Barnes:** "Way" is the journey of life. "Undefiled" means perfect or sincere (the same word as in Job 1:1). Walking in the law means obeying it as a habit. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/119-1.html
- **Gill:** These people are blameless before others and sincere before God. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/119-1.html
- **NET:** translates "whose actions are blameless." https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Psa&chapter=119
- **Where traditions differ (blamelessness):**
  - *Calvin (Reformed):* Does this rule out everyone who doesn't obey perfectly? If so, only angels would be blessed. God's children keep the free forgiveness of their sins, so they are blessed while still needing mercy. He links this to Ps 32:2. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/119-1.html
  - *Clarke (Methodist):* Reads the Hebrew as "the perfect ones." He means those who sincerely believe God's word, keep his ordinances, and have hearts and lives ruled by love, fear and obedience. He doesn't take up Calvin's question on this page. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/119-1.html

**v. 2**
- **Guzik:** "Keep" means doing, not just hearing. Seeking God with the whole heart has to include his word, or other spiritual practices can drift off course. The challenge is aimed at the divided heart, not the broken one (Spurgeon). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-119/
- **Calvin:** God isn't satisfied with outward service; he wants honest affection from the heart. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/119-1.html
- **Spurgeon:** David found for himself the blessedness he saw in others (he points to vv. 54–56 and 168). https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps119_001-008.cfm

**v. 3**
- **Guzik:** These people are marked by purity. They learn God's ways from his word, and God also gives the grace to walk in them. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-119/
- **NET:** "follow in his footsteps." https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Psa&chapter=119
- **Bible.org:** God's "ways" are his typical way of acting, set against ours. https://bible.org/seriespage/psalm-119-priority-god%E2%80%99s-word

**v. 4**
- **Guzik:** Here the psalmist starts praying to God, and keeps praying through most of the psalm. Spurgeon notes that God tells us to keep his rules, not to make up new ones. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-119/
- **Barnes:** The duty rests on God's command, not on human prudence or self-interest. That is the foundation of true virtue. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/psalms-119.html
- **Treasury of David:** Paying attention to Scripture isn't optional; God commands it earnestly. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tod/psalms-119.html
- **Homiletics material:** "Diligently" means careful, prompt, wholehearted obedience driven by love. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/tod/psalms/119.htm

**v. 5**
- **Guzik:** This is a prayer for the ability to obey, not just a pious wish. Boice notes that the psalmist isn't yet the blessed man he describes. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-119/
- **Spurgeon (older writer he quotes):** Seeing God's charge, David feels his own weakness. He wants to obey "by the spirit" but can't "by the flesh." https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps119_001-008.cfm
- **Barnes:** A constant desire to keep God's law is the mark of a godly person. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/psalms-119.html
- **NET:** "If only I were predisposed…" https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Psa&chapter=119

**v. 6**
- **Guzik:** Compared with God's word, we feel ashamed, and the psalmist prays for power to live without shame. Manton (via Spurgeon) separates the shame of a guilty conscience from the shame of a tender one. Poole and Bridges say "all your commandments" means no picking and choosing; we aim at all of them even though we can't obey perfectly. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-119/
- **NET:** "if I were focused on all your commands." https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Psa&chapter=119

**v. 7**
- **Guzik:** Praise has to come from an upright life, not be a moment or an image of praise. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-119/
- **Spurgeon's notes:** Even the best of God's servants are still students: "when I shall have learned." https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps119_001-008.cfm
- **NET:** "sincere thanks." https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Psa&chapter=119

**v. 8**
- **Guzik:** He senses desperation; without God the psalmist would be lost. Bridges says we may be forsaken for a time, but never "utterly" (compare Peter with Judas). Horne says only the "true David," Christ, could fully say "I will keep your statutes." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-119/
- **Gill (Baptist, Calvinist):** This resolve is made in the strength of grace. David doesn't expect to obey perfectly, and doesn't rely on obedience for life and salvation. Gill rejects a Jewish reading that puts "forsake me not" in brackets. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/119-8.html
- **Treasury of David:** He resolves to obey, but knows his weaknesses and prays not to be abandoned. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tod/psalms-119.html

## Beth (vv. 9–16)

**v. 9**
- **Guzik:** Young men face particular pressures (energy, independence, sexual maturity, money, peers, the spirit of the age). Boice: begin living for God as early as possible. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-119/
- **Spurgeon (quoted on Precept Austin):** Common sense asks the question, but only God can answer it and give the power to carry it out. https://www.preceptaustin.org/psalm-119-commentary
- **Barnes:** If a young man makes God's law his rule of life, it will never fail to keep him pure. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/119-9.html
- **Clarke:** "Way" can mean a rut or track: a young sinner's private habits of sin. Cleansing starts by admitting the way is impure and examining it by God's word. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/119-9.html
- **Calvin:** Nothing in life is pure until a person gives himself completely to God's word. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/119-9.html
- **Where traditions differ (what cleanses?):**
  - *Gill:* Prefers the rendering "by observing what is according to your word." The word shows how sinners are cleansed by Christ's blood and declared right by his righteousness, and how the Spirit makes them holy through the word. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/119-9.html
  - *Chuck Smith:* Links the verse to John 15:3 ("clean through the word"). https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/119-1.html
- **Keil & Delitzsch:** Explain the Hebrew as keeping one's way pure by guarding oneself. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/119-11.htm
- **NET:** "How can a young person maintain a pure life?" https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Psa&chapter=119

**v. 10**
- **Pulpit Commentary:** The prayer is not to stray by accident or ignorance. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/119.htm
- **Matthew Henry:** The tempter makes people think obeying God's word is up to them; a good man's desire matches God's command. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/psalms/119.htm
- **Henry Morris (on Precept Austin):** The young man, now less self-confident, asks for strength not to wander. https://www.preceptaustin.org/psalm-119-commentary
- **Chuck Smith:** Many people seek God half-heartedly. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/119-1.html
- **Clarke:** Every affection must be involved; keeping an idol in the heart blocks answered prayer. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/clarke/psalms/119.htm

**v. 11**
- **Barnes:** "Hid" means treasured, like hoarded jewels. Unseen, it became the secret power that governed him. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/119-11.htm
- **Gill:** He not only heard the word but believed it and stored it up. Its commands, promises and teachings all work against sin (2 Cor 7:1). https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/119-11.html
- **Calvin:** David models the path for all of us. With God's law deep in the heart, we're well defended against Satan's schemes. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/119-11.html
- **Geneva notes:** Similar to Calvin. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/119-11.htm
- **Pulpit:** Reads "your promise" (Hebrew *imrah*); a promise stored in the heart guards against being caught off guard by sin. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/119-11.htm
- **Cambridge Bible:** "Laid up," as a safeguard; compare Jer 31:33. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/119-11.htm
- **Keil & Delitzsch:** The word is kept in the heart as an inner driving force, not only as an outward rule. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/119-11.htm
- **A sermon at the top of the Bible Hub page** (unsigned there; the sermon index lists Alexander Maclaren's "Life Hid and not Hid"):
  - "Heart" means the centre of the whole self.
  - It widens "word" to God's will shown in providence, and then to Christ, the living Word.
  - It pairs the verse with Ps 40:10: what is hidden inside must show in how we live and what we say.
  - https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/119-11.htm and https://biblehub.com/sermons/psalms/119-11.htm
- **Chuck Smith:** Jesus answered Satan's temptations with "It is written"; the word is power against temptation. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/119-1.html
- **G. Campbell Morgan (quoted on Precept Austin):** the best book, in the best place, for the best purpose. https://www.preceptaustin.org/psalm-119-commentary
- **NET:** "store up." https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Psa&chapter=119

**v. 12**
- **Poole:** God is infinitely blessed, so let him bless me by teaching me, both to know and to practise. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/poole/psalms/119.htm
- **Keil & Delitzsch:** The poet moves from worship to request. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/119-11.htm
- **Chuck Smith:** The psalm has spoken of the blessed man; now it is "blessed are You." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/119-1.html
- **NET:** "You deserve praise." https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Psa&chapter=119

**v. 13**
- **Pulpit:** The word hidden in the heart naturally rises to the lips; Israelites were commanded to teach it (Deut 6:7). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/119.htm
- **Keil & Delitzsch:** The verb means recounting, as in Deut 6:7. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/119-11.htm
- **Matthew Henry:** Those fed with the bread of life should feed others with their lips. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/119-11.htm

**v. 14**
- **Homiletics outline:** Whatever riches are good for, God's testimonies do better: they meet the soul's needs and bring the highest joy. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/tod/psalms/119.htm
- **Matthew Henry:** The way of God's commands holds the unsearchable riches of Christ. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/119-11.htm
- **Keil & Delitzsch:** Read "as over all riches." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/119-11.htm
- **NET:** "the lifestyle prescribed by your rules." https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Psa&chapter=119

**vv. 15–16**
- **Treasury of David:** Three movements of the soul: meditation, then consideration, then delight. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tod/psalms-119.html
- **Guzik:** God's word fills the mind (meditate), the heart (delight) and the habits (not forget). https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/guzik_david/StudyGuide2017-Psa/Psa-119.cfm
- **Matthew Henry:** Meditation is useless unless good thoughts produce good works. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/119-11.htm
- **NET notes:**
  - The verb forms in v. 15 express resolve.
  - "Regard" is literally "gaze at," and "ways" means God's own behaviour.
  - The verbs in v. 16 stress a lasting attitude, though "I will…" is also possible.
  - https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Psa&chapter=119

## Gimel (vv. 17–24)

**v. 17**
- **NET:** "Be kind to your servant! Then I will live and keep your instructions." https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Psa&chapter=119

**v. 18**
- **Piper (Baptist, on Precept Austin):**
  - We must give up self-reliance and ask the Spirit to make us feel the wonder of what is already in Scripture, not to reveal new things.
  - Prayer for understanding and hard thinking go together; neither works alone.
  - God shows Christ's beauty to those who look into his word.
  - https://www.preceptaustin.org/psalm_11918_commentary
- **Same page, other comments:**
  - The prayer admits spiritual dimness, and that only God can cure it.
  - The psalmist asks for clearer sight, not a new faculty.
  - The "natural man" can't discover these wonders.
  - https://www.preceptaustin.org/psalm_11918_commentary
- **Chuck Smith:** Pray this before reading Scripture, citing 1 Cor 2:14. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/119-1.html
- **Homiletics outline:** Man's blindness hides the wonders of the Bible. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/tod/psalms/119.htm
- **NET:** "so I can truly see." https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Psa&chapter=119

**v. 19**
- **NET:** "like a foreigner in this land." https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Psa&chapter=119

**v. 20**
- **NET note:** The Hebrew is literally "my soul languishes for longing." https://classic.net.bible.org/verse.php?book=psa&chapter=119&verse=20
- **Barnes:** This longing was steady and habitual, not occasional. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/psalms-119.html
- **Spurgeon outline ("Holy Longings"):** The desire itself shows God at work and makes Christ precious. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/tod/psalms/119.htm

**v. 21**
- **Spurgeon outline:** The character of the proud, God's dealings with them, and our relation to them. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/tod/psalms/119.htm
- **NET:** "Those who stray… are doomed." https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Psa&chapter=119

**vv. 22–23**
- **NET:** "Spare me shame and humiliation"; "Though rulers plot and slander me." https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Psa&chapter=119

**v. 24**
- **Chuck Smith:** He turns to the word for counsel and guidance. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/119-1.html
- **NET:** "they give me guidance." https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Psa&chapter=119

## Daleth (vv. 25–29)

**v. 25**
- **Homiletics:** Sitting in the dust is the posture of humiliation, possibly recalling sackcloth and ashes, and fits the psalmist's low spiritual state. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/psalms/119.htm
- **Precept Austin:** Ties the prayer "revive me" to Ps 19:7 (the law restores the soul) and to vv. 107 and 149. https://www.preceptaustin.org/psalm-119-commentary
- **NET:** "I collapse in the dirt. Revive me with your word!" https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Psa&chapter=119

**v. 26**
- **Precept Austin:** Likens this to a patient telling the doctor his symptoms and the doctor prescribing; sin is a disease only the great Physician cures. https://www.preceptaustin.org/psalm-119-commentary
- **NET note:** The Hebrew is literally "my ways I proclaimed." https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Psa&chapter=119

**v. 27**
- **Spurgeon outline ("The Student's Prayer"):** Applies the verse to training for ministry: the student learns, then the preacher speaks. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/tod/psalms/119.htm
- **NET note:** Literally "the way of your precepts make me understand." https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Psa&chapter=119

**v. 28**
- **Chuck Smith:** When we're ready to give up, the word gives strength. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/119-1.html
- **NET:** "I collapse from grief. Sustain me by your word!" https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Psa&chapter=119

**v. 29**
- **NET:** "Graciously give me your law!" https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Psa&chapter=119

---

**Some useful links:** Guzik's sections for vv. 17–24 and 25–32 are https://enduringword.com/psalm-11917-24-gimel-the-greatness-and-glory-of-gods-word/ and https://enduringword.com/psalm-11925-32-daleth-the-greatness-and-glory-of-gods-word/ (video pages I didn't read). The verse-by-verse Bible Hub and StudyLight commentary pages, numbered 119-17 to 119-29, would fill in most of the gaps for vv. 17–29.
